item.title: Arita Ceramics Fair — Guide
item.description: The Arita Ceramics Fair (Arita Toki-ichi), held every year during Golden Week (roughly 29 April–5 May), is the largest and most famous pottery market in Japan. For a week, the main street of the historic porcelain town of Arita — birthplace of Japanese porcelain — is lined for some four kilometres with hundreds of stalls, as kilns, wholesalers and shops sell everything from everyday tableware to fine art pieces, often at significant discounts and bargain prices.

item.title: Hakata Dontaku Port Festival — Guide
item.description: The Hakata Dontaku Port Festival, held each year on May 3–4 during Golden Week, is one of Japan’s most-attended festivals, drawing over two million people. With roots going back centuries to New Year celebrations, it has grown into a joyful, participatory city-wide event: a huge citizens' parade fills the main street with thousands of participants from local groups, companies and schools, dancing and performing in costume. A signature sight is people clapping wooden shamoji rice scoops together in rhythm as they dance.

item.title: Hiroshima Flower Festival: Golden Week on Peace Boulevard — Guide
item.description: The Hiroshima Flower Festival, held over three days of Golden Week each May, is the city’s largest annual celebration and draws well over a million people. Begun in 1977, it fills the broad Peace Boulevard with flower-decked floats, marching bands, dance teams and stages of music running from the city centre toward the Peace Park, culminating in a huge floral monument. Its founding spirit was explicitly one of peace and recovery, and the effect is striking: the same city that mourns each August turns bright, loud and joyful in spring, and the festival is free and open to everyone.

item.title: Hamamatsu Kite Festival: Giant Kite Battles Over the Dunes — Guide
item.description: The Hamamatsu Festival, held every year over Golden Week (3–5 May), is famous for its giant kite battles, in which more than a hundred neighbourhood teams fly enormous kites — some several metres across, each painted with their district’s emblem — above the Nakatajima sand dunes, deliberately crossing lines to cut rivals from the sky amid trumpet fanfares and chanting. The tradition began as a celebration of firstborn children and continues today, with evenings bringing a second spectacle as ornately carved palace-like floats parade through the city streets.

item.title: Naha Hari Guide: Okinawa's Dragon Boat Race & Dates
item.description: The Naha Hari (Haarii) is one of Okinawa’s great seasonal spectacles — a colourful dragon boat festival held at Naha Port over Golden Week (May 3–5). Crews paddle ornate dragon-prowed boats called haarii-bune in thunderous races that pray for maritime safety and a good catch, a tradition with centuries-old roots and Chinese ties. With races, food stalls, music and fireworks, it’s a lively, family-friendly festival and a great reason to be in Naha in early May.
